label: sec:rigid-monoidal-intro
html:
Why do the axioms of a physical theory land on a rigid braided monoidal category? Two lines of thought converge here. Composing physical processes in sequence and in parallel forces a monoidal structure. Superselection-sector analysis of local observables forces the same. Any compositional theory of physical systems settles into this framework, which we fix before stating the quantum-universe axioms.

This section defines the two structures separately, because the paper uses them at two different levels. A quantum universe is braided: it has interactions. A quantum observable universe is braided and rigid: it also has duals, hence antiparticles and closed knots.

We keep two examples in view: the polynomial ring \mathbb{C}[z] and the coordinate ring \mathcal{O}(\mathrm{SU}(2)). Objects have tensor products and a unit over a base ring, making the category R-linear. In the rigid case every object V has a dual V^{\vee}, and the zig-zag (snake) equations make V^{\vee} a right dual. A braiding exchanges tensor factors. The symmetric case c_{Y,X} \circ c_{X,Y} = \mathrm{id} marks the classical limit.

The next section mounts the Frobenius--Hopf object, the fibre functor, and the differential calculus on this scaffold.
